title: Group-theoretic treatment of strong light-matter coupling with an arbitrary number of excitations
authors: Antti Peltola, Olli Siltanen, Kimmo Luoma, Konstantinos S. Daskalakis
abstract: Strong light-matter interactions in optical microcavities give rise to hybrid light-matter states known as polaritons. While actively used in modern technologies, theoretical descriptions of such systems are often restricted to the single-excitation case, limiting their ability to capture many-excitation physics and hindering further technological advancements. Here, by exploiting the combinatorial structure of quantum emitters, we investigate the Tavis-Cummings model with arbitrary number of excitations. We derive the structure and properties of its eigensystem and identify allowed radiative transitions in systems of realistic size scales. Our work reveals new behavior inaccessible to the few-excitation regime, while also providing a framework to reduce the computational complexity of similar systems with exponentially growing Hilbert spaces.
summary: This paper develops a group-theoretic method to solve the spectrum of the Tavis-Cummings model for an arbitrary number of excitations. By exploiting the symmetry of the Hamiltonian, the authors manage the exponentially growing Hilbert space, providing exact predictions for polariton physics. This framework is crucial for advancing theoretical understanding of strongly coupled quantum light-matter systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the theoretical challenge of extending the description of strong light-matter coupling (polaritons) from the limited single-excitation case to systems involving an arbitrary number of excitations.
main_result: The authors developed a group-theoretic framework that allows for the exact calculation of the spectrum and eigenstates for arbitrary numbers of excitations, revealing new physics inaccessible in simpler regimes.
method: The core method involves exploiting the symmetry of the Tavis-Cummings Hamiltonian using representation theory (Schur-Weyl duality) to decompose the exponentially large Hilbert space into manageable, irreducible blocks.
model_or_system: The system models $N$ two-level quantum emitters coupled uniformly to a single optical cavity mode, described by the Tavis-Cummings Hamiltonian under the Rotating-Wave Approximation. The analysis focuses on the conserved total excitation number $X$.
key_observables: Eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian ($E^{(X,m)}_k$), average excitation contents ($\langle n_c angle, \langle n_{TLS} angle$), and transition probabilities between excitation manifolds.
important_parameters: The number of emitters ($N$), the total excitation number ($X$), and the symmetry index ($m$). The analysis is particularly focused on the resonant condition ($E_{TLS} = E_c$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Rotating-Wave Approximation (RWA), which conserves the total excitation number $X$, and utilizes asymptotic limits ($N 	o \infty$) for certain calculations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dimension distribution of irreducible representations $V^{(X)}_m$ for large $N$, and plot the evolution of emission energy versus excitation number $X$, showing a collapse towards the cavity energy $E_c$ when $X > N/2$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically builds the theoretical framework by first establishing the symmetry decomposition of the Hilbert space using group theory. It then derives the structure of the reduced interaction matrix, calculates the eigenvalues and average excitation contents for small $X$, and finally analyzes asymptotic limits to determine transition probabilities and multiplicity distributions.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, generalizable theoretical tool for analyzing complex, many-body quantum optical systems, moving beyond the standard few-excitation approximations that limit technological modeling.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic illustration of the system, model, and predictions. The Hilbert space corresponding to the physical system (two-level systems and cavity mode) grows exponentially with the excitation number X. This growth, however, remains computationally manageable when exploiting the algebraic structure of the Hilbert space. The structure, visualized here by the Young tableaux, manifests itself as symmetries in the eigenenergies (dispersion curves) and observable transition energies (wavy arrows) of the system.

Figure 2: Dimensions of the irreps V (X) m for N = 1000 for X ∈{150, 300, 400, 500}. In (a–b) the dark states dominate in multiplicity, while dark polaritons become progressively comparable with growing X. In (c) the dark polaritons overtake the dark states. In (d) the dark states disappear completely, and the dark polaritons end up in a smooth distribution peaked at high m. Panel (e) shows the logarithms of the X = 500 dimensions, revealing the relative sizes invisible to the linear plots.

Figure 3: Eigenvalue distributions of A for N = 1000 and X ∈{3, 10, 75, 350, 450, 500}. Panels (a–c) are in logarithmic scale and 0 ≤m ≤X, showing a trade-off between the multiplicity and energy density for high and low m. Panels (d–f) show linearly for 0.8X ≤m ≤X, how the statistically most relevant states compare at high excitation numbers. The distributions represent a unitless, centered-around-zero energy spectrum for the system, scalable to arbitrary ET LS = Ec and g. The TLS excitation content of the states is proportional to m, such that red points have higher photonic content, and black points refer to dark states.
